rationale: B wins because it keeps the heat on what is provable instead of decorating the gaps. Its best line, "the most newsworthy fact is what is NOT yet known (the post-relaunch paying-user trend)," is exactly the disciplined investor/turnaround frame this update can support. A has strong bones, but "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" overclaims from one Bumble relaunch, and "her first fix is AI" treats an unsupported sequencing claim like fact.
gaps_in_A: "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" is a category claim the update does not prove; A admits it needs outside evidence, but the headline still sells the conclusion too hard.
"her first fix is AI" / "first major public move" is plausible, but not supplied. The facts say the relaunch is under the returning CEO, not that this is her first fix or first major move.

"Bumble's defense of its 'authentic,' women-first model" smuggles in "authentic" as Bumble's positioning. The update says women-message-first remains core and users criticize AI as inauthentic, not that Bumble claims authenticity as its defense.
The next step says `find-journalists`; that is close, but a fit check should come after choosing and proving the angle, not just list-building by beat.
gaps_in_B: "the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is color, but it risks lazy founder-return pattern-matching without evidence that Bumble's situation maps cleanly to those cases.
"A tech-business feature reporter at a national outlet" is better than vague "tech journalist," but still broad; the strongest versions would name tighter desk types without naming journalists.

"Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" implies plural category movement. B catches itself with the caution that Bumble is one data point, but the headline still reaches beyond the supplied facts.
